editions.title: Microsoft quits Nscale site as iPhone Duo and AI trade wobble dominate
editions.intro:
The biggest story is a reported setback for Nscale, the British AI cloud startup. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first UK data centre in Loughton, Essex, weeks before Nscale's planned IPO seeking up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, while Microsoft has not commented. The report also points to grid connection delays and wider investor caution towards neocloud firms, with CoreWeave shares reported lower.

The wider backdrop is a jittery AI trade. Bloomberg reports that a deepening selloff in US technology shares is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI supply chain, as rising financing costs could curb data-centre and hardware spending. The Financial Times asks whether Meta's earnings can restore confidence in AI investment, and a separate FT piece argues that America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical limits. Against that, SemiAnalysis suggests more than 300 local data centre moratoriums have delayed only a small slice of US buildout.

Apple dominates the product news. Reports say the iPhone Duo foldable is sold out for months, that store staff have been told walk-in buyers should not expect stock, and that Apple's pre-order rollout across more than 70 countries was a mistake, according to Mark Gurman. Apple has also published the Duo's battery label, and a store refresh on 6 November is expected to coincide with new products including a touchscreen MacBook Pro. Most of these remain unconfirmed rumours.

top_stories.summary: Bloomberg's Mark Gurman argues Apple opened pre-orders in more than 70 countries despite knowing supply was tight. Estimated shipping dates have slipped to around late January in most markets.

editions.title: Microsoft Walks Away From Nscale Site as Neocloud Nerves Grow
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the day is Microsoft's reported withdrawal from an anchor deal for Nscale's first British data centre in Loughton, Essex. The Telegraph says Microsoft has pulled out weeks before the AI cloud startup's planned IPO, which is reported to seek up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, while Microsoft has not commented. Grid connection delays at the site were also reported, and the story is being read as a sign of wider caution toward neocloud firms.

That caution fed into a broader theme of AI-trade nerves. Bloomberg reports that a deepening selloff in US tech shares is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI supply chain, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The Financial Times, meanwhile, argues America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical limits of power, equipment and money. Investors will look to Meta's earnings next, which the FT frames as a test of whether confidence in the AI spending boom can be restored.

Elsewhere, Ericsson beat expectations with third-quarter adjusted EBITA of SEK 10.1bn against a consensus of SEK 7.93bn, and its shares rose as much as 11% in Stockholm. On the chip front, a single unverified report says Nvidia wants Samsung, Micron and SK hynix to build custom HBM base dies on TSMC's 3nm process, while a separate rumour suggests China could let major firms buy H200 chips under tight caps. Both remain unconfirmed.

editions.title: Nvidia RTX 5090 Row, TSMC Profit Record and Starlink Limits Dominate
editions.intro: TSMC posted a record quarterly profit, with demand for AI chips still far outstripping supply, but it signalled caution on 2027. Meanwhile, the AI trade showed strain: Asian chip suppliers were exposed to a US tech selloff, and reports that OpenAI's revenue trails expectations added to nerves. Ukraine's dispute with SpaceX over Starlink speed limits escalated, with Zelenskyy calling the restrictions deliberate. Apple's iPhone Duo faced shortages and Apple's chief executive called memory supply a crisis.

top_stories.title: TSMC records sixth straight record profit, cautious on 2027
top_stories.summary: TSMC reported record third-quarter net profit of NT$763.1bn, up 69%, with revenue up 51%. It guided to about 44% dollar revenue growth in 2026, but chairman C.C. Wei warned that price-sensitive consumer markets are under pressure and that the company is being prudent about 2027.

top_stories.title: Starshield speed limits cut Ukrainian interceptor drones
top_stories.summary: Speed limits on SpaceX's Starshield network reportedly cut links for interceptor drones above about 161 km/h, forcing Ukrainian units to cancel missions. Reports suggest the order came from the White House or was discussed by Musk and Trump, but these claims are unverified.

top_stories.title: Apple's Ternus calls memory shortage a crisis
top_stories.summary: Apple's chief executive told TIME that memory chip constraints are a crisis and all options should be considered. The comments follow a report that Apple tested memory chips from a Chinese firm, which prompted US warnings against them.

top_stories.title: Microsoft plans multi-gigawatt Maia 300 rollout
top_stories.summary: Microsoft plans to scale its Maia accelerators to multi-gigawatt deployments from 2027, with Maia 300 as its primary inference system. Analysts expect Maia to be only about 10% of its AI chip spend by early 2027, so Nvidia's position is not yet under threat.

top_stories.title: Intel confirms Razor Lake-AX timing and 700 TOPS target
top_stories.summary: Intel SVP Cho Min-sung confirmed Nova Lake for 2027 and Razor Lake-AX for 2028, the latter targeting 700 TOPS of AI compute. The aim is premium devices and physical AI.

top_stories.title: Tesla shows fan-powered Roadster, production 2028
top_stories.summary: Tesla demonstrated its next-generation Roadster using powered fans and a retractable rear wing for downforce. Musk said production begins in 2028, with reservations open at $50,000 for the base model and $250,000 for the Thrust trim.

rumour_watch.note: A reported $20bn revenue shortfall at OpenAI, relayed without a named source. Plausible given the market backdrop, but it is an internal figure and OpenAI has not confirmed it.
Nvidia's Jeff Fisher reportedly denied the RTX 5090 is discontinued, citing tight supply. Credible on the record, but retailer listings at inflated prices suggest supply is genuinely thin.
Reported FTC demands aimed at OpenAI and Anthropic. Only a feed summary, and the story stresses it is not a finding of wrongdoing, so treat as unconfirmed.
DeepSeek says its new Flash model beats larger rivals on agentic tasks. Weights are public, but independent benchmarks are still pending.

editions.title: Chip stocks extend slide as TSMC posts record profit and Apple's Duo sells out
editions.intro: Semiconductor shares suffered their longest losing streak since 2006, with the Philadelphia index down more than 12% in a week and short sellers pocketing an estimated $32bn. The mood was sharply different at TSMC, which reported a record quarterly profit but warned of caution on 2027. Apple's foldable iPhone Duo went on sale to strong demand, with delivery dates slipping into 2027.

top_stories.title: Chip stocks suffer longest losing streak since 2006
top_stories.summary: The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell over 12% in seven days and was on course for an eighth straight loss. Short sellers have made an estimated $32bn in paper gains, according to S3 Partners.

top_stories.title: TSMC records sixth straight profit but turns cautious on 2027
top_stories.summary: Third-quarter net profit hit a record NT$763.1bn, up 69%, and 2026 dollar revenue growth is guided to about 44%. Chairman C.C. Wei warned that consumer markets face pressure from rising component costs, while AI demand still outstrips supply.

top_stories.title: Apple launches iPhone Duo foldable from $1,999
top_stories.summary: The foldable has a 5.4-inch outer and 7.6-inch inner display, with Touch ID on the power button. Apple calls pre-order demand extraordinary, and online delivery estimates have slipped into late January.

top_stories.title: Dell sees memory shortage worsening into 2027
top_stories.summary: Michael Dell expects HBM and DRAM shortages to get worse next year, with supply constraints lasting up to four years. Dell holds a record $95bn of back-ordered AI and enterprise server orders.

top_stories.title: Eight US states sue OpenAI over ChatGPT harm to children
top_stories.summary: Attorneys general in eight states filed lawsuits on 14 October under consumer protection and public nuisance laws. They seek court-ordered changes to ChatGPT, civil penalties and a bar on developing self-improving models.

FT-sourced report that SoftBank is in talks for Allied Universal; a major outlet, but size and timing are unknown and no deal is announced.
Korean report of Galaxy S27 Ultra overheating on Snapdragon; Qualcomm has denied it, so credibility is mixed and the Exynos switch is undecided.

Finance.title: Gulf conflict lifts oil as markets weigh Middle East risk
Finance.summary:
The most market-relevant story is the escalating Saudi-led fight with Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. An airstrike in Saada reportedly killed at least nine people, Egypt's National Defence Council pledged support to Saudi Arabia, and President el-Sissi has asked parliament for authority to deploy troops abroad. Iran says it is reviewing a US response to its proposal to end the eight-month war. Energy stocks and crude have risen on the back of wider conflict, and a Financial Times-style report on tanker rates suggests shipping costs are adding substantially to oil prices.

Elsewhere, markets are wrestling with a rising rate backdrop. The 10-year US Treasury yield has moved above 5% for the first time in almost two decades, and options traders are positioning for a jump in the VIX as US inflation accelerates and AI-linked shares wobble. In the UK, reports that GDP unexpectedly rose have strengthened the pound, while Bank of England policymakers debate how many further rate rises are needed and whether a November hike is on the table.

Corporate and policy news is also busy. AT&T is selling AT&T Mexico to a group including Grupo Televisa, Carefour reports around 50 stores ransacked in French riots, and China has proposed export controls on 12 solar manufacturing technologies. Attention on Starlink is rising too, with restrictions in Ukraine and a US threat to Europe over limits on the service.

World.title: France's protests turn violent as Macron faces pressure
World.summary:
Nationwide protests in France over the cost of living and school conditions turned violent on Saturday, with reported arrests of around 1,800 to over 2,000, widespread property damage and a historic town hall in Limoges largely destroyed by fire. Estimates of attendance vary sharply, with the interior ministry citing 550,000 and the CGT union 800,000. Politicians from left and right have called for the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, to resign, and the government is due to hold a crisis meeting on Monday, with President Macron expected to address the nation.

The unrest comes roughly six months before presidential elections, and political figures are already trading blame. Some ministers and far-right figures have pointed to ultra-left groups, while critics say the state was caught off guard. Similar housing and cost-of-living protests have spread to Italy, Portugal and Albania, suggesting a broader wave of public frustration across Europe.

For markets, the main channel is French political risk. CAC 40 weakness and pressure on the euro are the most visible signs so far, and any sign of a shift in government or fiscal policy ahead of the 2027 vote could weigh on French assets. Energy markets are also being driven by the Russia-Ukraine strikes on oil infrastructure, with crude prices firmer after drone attacks in St Petersburg and US sanctions relief for Russia under review.

points.text: Trump described France as 'burning', adding an international dimension to the domestic unrest in Paris.
Russia and Ukraine are trading strikes on energy sites after Trump's 'energy ceasefire' broke down, with Ukrainian drones hitting St Petersburg oil facilities.
Rubio says the US waiver on Russia sanctions lasts 60 days, citing energy price pressures from the Iran war and Houthi attacks.
Drone attacks on Black Sea shipping have intensified, with a tanker set ablaze off Romania and seven crew reported missing.
Albania's Tirana protests entered a sixth day, with PM Edi Rama refusing to resign and citing a 'foreign hand'.
Egypt's defence leadership pledged support for Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks, with Sisi seeking lawmakers' approval for assistance.

Tech.title: Microsoft reportedly quits Nscale UK site before IPO
Tech.summary:
The most consequential tech story today is a reported pullback by Microsoft from anchoring Nscale's first British data centre in Loughton, Essex. The Telegraph reports the move comes as the AI cloud start-up prepares an IPO seeking up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, while Microsoft has not commented. Grid connection delays at the site are also mentioned, and the story sits within wider investor caution about neocloud firms.

Alongside this, the wider AI trade is looking shakier. Bloomberg reports that a deepening selloff in US technology shares is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI supply chain, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The FT argues America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical-world limits, while SemiAnalysis finds that more than 300 local data-centre moratoriums have delayed only a small share of projects. Meta's earnings are seen as a test of investor confidence in the AI spending boom.

Elsewhere, Apple dominates the consumer news flow. Reports on the foldable iPhone Duo describe extraordinary pre-order demand, shipping dates slipping into January and store staff warning walk-in buyers. Rumours point to a touchscreen MacBook around 6 November and a 9-inch robotic HomeView for 2027 or 2028. Nvidia and Samsung feature in reports on custom HBM and a possible chip switch, and Anthropic and Google face new AI policy and legal stories.

points.text: Apple reportedly cut iPhone 18 Pro orders by up to 20%, though the claim is unverified and has no named source.
Samsung may switch from Snapdragon to its own Exynos for the Galaxy S27 Ultra over reported overheating; Qualcomm denies it.
Nvidia reportedly asked Samsung, Micron and SK hynix to make custom HBM base dies on TSMC's 3nm node, citing 30% more bandwidth.
Accenture is reportedly looking to sell its China operations for up to $1.5bn, according to the Financial Times.
China could reportedly allow Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek to buy capped volumes of Nvidia's H200 chips; unconfirmed.
Anthropic is working with law firms on fair negotiation norms for AI agents, after tests showed stronger models win better deals.

Fashion.title: Luxury shares slide as China and US demand soften
Fashion.summary:
The luxury sector dominates today's fashion business news, with several stories pointing to sustained pressure on the big groups. Shares in LVMH, Hermès and Kering have reportedly fallen by up to 40% so far this year, and commentary from The Business of Fashion and an opinion piece from UA.NEWS links the weakness to a difficult period of weak numbers, leadership gaps and a possible slowdown in US spending. LVMH is also reported to be rethinking its approach in China, where a visible logo no longer guarantees sales, while Chanel is opening its first Wuhan store at SKP as luxury brands in China close weak outlets and test new regional markets.

Elsewhere, the cost and retail picture is mixed. The Footwear Distributors & Retailers of America warns that higher oil, freight and energy costs could push shoe prices up again from autumn 2026, with Under Armour and Nike seen as more exposed than Birkenstock, Deckers, Crocs and On Running. Beauty groups face their own scrutiny: Estée Lauder agreed a $210 million settlement in a China daigou sales shareholder lawsuit, and investors are weighing whether Estée Lauder and Coty can justify their focus on cash over growth.

Other items are smaller. Chanel's destruction of unsold stock is facing a reported crackdown, Pink is taking the halftime slot at the Victoria's Secret show, and Veronica Leoni is leaving Calvin Klein. Several fashion-week reports from India, Dubai, Nigeria and New York add colour but little market impact.

points.text: The Business of Fashion describes weak numbers and empty chairs across luxury, pointing to pressure on performance and management.
The Business of Fashion warns that the US, a key source of luxury demand, may be losing momentum.
Estée Lauder has agreed a $210 million settlement in a China daigou sales shareholder lawsuit, without a trial.
A Los Angeles Times report says Chanel shredded thousands of unsold items, with the practice now reportedly facing a crackdown.
Pink takes the Victoria's Secret show halftime slot, citing five straight quarters of growth and a Marshmallow bra launch.
Veronica Leoni is leaving Calvin Klein after four seasons, though no successor or reasons were given.
